chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Safwan from 'Abdullah from al-Halabi said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the divorce of the drunkard and his manumission, so he said, 'It is not valid.' He said, 'And I asked him about the divorce of the ma'tuh (insane person),' so he said, 'And what is it?' I said, 'The fool who has lost his mind.' He said, 'It is not valid.' I said, 'So is the woman like that? Is her sale and purchase valid?' He said, 'No.'

key_terms.اَلذَّاهِبُ اَلْعَقْلِ: The one who has lost his mind
key_terms.اَلْأَحْمَقُ: The fool (often used in fiqh to denote a person with limited mental capacity)
key_terms.اَلْمَعْتُوهِ: The insane person (one of unsound mind)

ai.seo_question: Is the divorce of a drunkard or insane person valid in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies that the legal incapacity (*ajz*) of a drunkard (*sakran*) and an insane person (*ma'tuh*) extends beyond divorce to include commercial transactions, establishing a consistent principle of diminished legal agency. This ruling underscores the Shia jurisprudential view that intoxication and insanity impair the cognitive capacity required for valid *ijab* and *qabul* in both marital and economic contracts. The hadith highlights the practical implication that such individuals cannot independently bind themselves in legal matters, a principle derived from their lack of full mental discernment.
